name: Montresso Art Foundation (Jardin Rouge)
overview: Artist residency and art space among olive groves about half an hour's drive from Marrakech, the last stretch through a village, run by the Montresso Art Foundation (Arterritory, Una Meistere, 16 February 2020); the foundation says it has been settled in Morocco since 2009 (Rivet).
A private initiative of the French collector and patron Jean-Louis Haguenauer, who bought the land in 2002; Jardin Rouge opened in 2009 (Arterritory).

The foundation has existed as a legal entity since 1981 and first held a collection begun in the 1980s; its patronage grew in the 1990s with creative workshops for young Russian artists, then group shows such as one at the Laennec hospital in Paris in September 2012 (director Estelle Guilié to Artribune, December 2021).
funding_verdict: Montresso Art Foundation (Jardin Rouge): private: the collector Jean-Louis Haguenauer's money, plus sales to a friends' circle

name: Le Cube – independent art room
overview: Independent exhibition, residency and research space at 2 rue Benzerte in Rabat, with exhibition, projection, conference, workshop and performance spaces, a library and a freely accessible archive (Le Cube).

Founded in 2005 by Elisabeth Piskernik, born in Vienna, who lives and works between Rabat and Vienna. It was founded with the artists' collective 212 (Amina Benbouchta, Hassan Echair, Safaa Erruas, Jamila Lamrani, Imad Mansour, Myriam Mihindou, Younes Rahmoun) (Le Cube).
Became Le Cube, independent art room in 2010. Afrik.com, on 24 January 2011, announced the inauguration of the new space for 2 February 2011.
funding_verdict: Le Cube: independent artist-run space, working with foreign cultural institutes and project partners

name: Museum Arnhem
overview: Municipal-origin museum of art and cultural history on Utrechtsestraat in Arnhem (Wikipedia, nl).

Founded in 1856. Earlier names Gemeentemuseum Arnhem and Museum voor Moderne Kunst Arnhem (MMKA). The collection grew from the estate of Alexander Ver Huell, who left his paintings, drawings, prints and decorative arts to the municipality when he died in 1897 (Wikipedia, nl).

The historic building was designed by Cornelis Outshoorn in 1873 as a gentlemen's club, mostly used by sugar planters returned from the Dutch East Indies. It passed to the Gemeentemuseum in 1920 because membership fell (Wikipedia, nl).
funding_verdict: Museum Arnhem: mainly public: Gemeente Arnhem

name: Fries Museum
overview: Museum of art, crafts and history of Fryslân on Wilhelminaplein in Leeuwarden, with a collection of about 1 million objects covering 1200 to 2000 (Wikipedia).
Founded on 13 April 1881 by a society for the preservation of Frisian culture, and first housed in the former Eysinga house on the Koningstraat (Wikipedia).

The present building on Wilhelminaplein was designed by Hubert-Jan Henket and opened on 13 September 2013 by Queen Máxima. The Frisian architect Abe Bonnema initiated it and left 18 million euros to the museum when he died in 2001 (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Fries Museum: funded by the Province of Fryslân, the municipality of Leeuwarden, Dutch funds and partners including the VriendenLoterij and Windpark Fryslân

name: Museum De Lakenhal
overview: Leiden's municipal museum of fine art and history, holding early works by Rembrandt, Lucas van Leyden's Last Judgement, De Stijl works, contemporary art and a collection of Dutch Golden Age fijnschilder paintings (Wikipedia).
Founded in 1874 as a municipal museum (Wikipedia).

The building was erected in 1640 by Arent van 's-Gravesande as a cloth hall, a guild hall for cloth merchants. An exhibition hall was added at the end of the 19th century and a new wing in 1922 (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Museum De Lakenhal: mainly public: Gemeente Leiden, with state and provincial money and a long list of funds and donors

name: Museum Beelden aan Zee
overview: Museum of modern and contemporary sculpture at Harteveltstraat 1 in Scheveningen, The Hague, on a side street off the boulevard. It calls itself the only museum in the Netherlands devoted exclusively to sculpture (Wikipedia, nl).
Founded in 1994 by the collectors Theo Scholten (1927 to 2005) and Lida Scholten-Miltenburg (1922 to 2026) (Wikipedia, nl; the museum's site notes her death).

Designed by the architect Wim Quist in sand-coloured concrete, glass, natural stone and wood. The museum lies in the dunes beneath the historic Paviljoen Von Wied, with a view of the sea (museum website).
funding_verdict: Museum Beelden aan Zee: private foundation with lottery support: the VriendenLoterij, its own assets and donations

name: Centraal Museum
overview: City museum of art, design, fashion and Utrecht history at Agnietenstraat 1, in the medieval Agnietenklooster near the Nicolaaskerkhof. The building is a Rijksmonument (Dutch Wikipedia).

A civic museum opened in Utrecht's city hall in 1830 and was open to the public from 1838. In 1921 it moved to the Agnietenklooster and merged several Utrecht collections, which gave it its name (Dutch Wikipedia). A 1987 extension (the former stable complex as exhibition space) and a 1999 glass entrance building were followed by a renovation from January 2014 that turned the entrance building into a museum café (Dutch Wikipedia).
Collection of over 50,000 objects, including about 8,000 fashion items and the largest collection of Rietveld designs (Dutch Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Centraal Museum: public partners, funds and corporate sponsors: Municipality of Utrecht, Dutch Ministry of Education, Culture and Science and VriendenLoterij; main sponsor Mercis bv

name: Tjibaou Cultural Centre (ADCK)
overview: Kanak cultural centre on the Tina Peninsula, about 8 km northeast of Nouméa's historic centre, between the lagoon and Boulari Bay (Wikipedia).

Run by the Agence de développement de la culture kanak (ADCK), which was formed in 1989 on the first anniversary of the Matignon-Oudinot Agreements and has its main base at the centre (Wikipedia). The centre was inaugurated on 4 May 1998 (Les Nouvelles Calédoniennes via dnc.nc).
Named for Jean-Marie Tjibaou, the independence leader assassinated in 1989, who had proposed a cultural centre (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Tjibaou Cultural Centre: public: run by the public agency ADCK, with the French State paying 68 percent of the 2025 renovation works

press_items.title: David Langdon, "AD Classics: Centre Culturel Jean-Marie Tjibaou / Renzo Piano Building Workshop" (2015)

name: Dunedin Public Art Gallery
overview: Public art gallery in The Octagon in central Dunedin, close to the public library, Dunedin Town Hall and the Regent Theatre (Wikipedia).

Founded in 1884 by W. M. Hodgkins. Wikipedia calls it the first public art gallery in New Zealand. It was moved between several buildings, into Queen's Gardens in 1907 and a Logan Park building in 1927 designed by Edmund Anscombe, which Sir Percy and Lady Sargood bought and gave to the city as a memorial to their son, killed at Gallipoli (Wikipedia).
The gallery moved to the refitted D.I.C. building in the Octagon in 1996 (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Dunedin Public Art Gallery: council-run: Dunedin City Council pays the running costs, with Creative New Zealand and private partners

name: The Dowse Art Museum
overview: Council-run public art and craft museum at 45 Laings Road, Lower Hutt.

Opened on 31 May 1971 as the Dowse Art Gallery. Renamed the Dowse Art Museum in 1981 under director James Mack (the museum's own history). The idea came in 1963 from the Hutt Art Society and Mayor Percy Dowse. The Hutt City Council voted for the gallery despite public opinion that the money was better spent on pensioners' flats and playgrounds (museum history).

Named for Percy Dowse, Mayor of Lower Hutt from 1950 to 1970 (museum history). Wikipedia adds that the building was first conceived as a memorial to his wife Mary Dowse, who died in a 1964 road accident.
funding_verdict: The Dowse Art Museum: mainly public: Hutt City Council

name: Toi Māori Aotearoa
overview: Charitable trust and national network of Māori artists, also called Māori Arts New Zealand, with a small Wellington team and office at Level 4, Change House, 150 Featherston Street (Toi Māori website, Annual Report 2024).

Founded in 1996: the trust deed is dated 14 October 1996 and the trust was set up by the chairs of eight national Māori art form committees, who elect the trustees (Annual Report 2024). It was publicly launched at "Patua: Māori Arts in Action", curated by Sandy Adsett at City Gallery Wellington (Toi Māori website).

Founding trustees named on its website include Hirini Moko Mead, Emily Rangitiaria Schuster, Tīmoti Kāretu, Dame Georgina Kirby and Trevor Horowaewae Maxwell. Current trustees listed there: Tracey Morgan (Chair), Robert Gabel (Deputy Chair), Ranui Ngarimu, Sir Derek Lardelli, Lady Rose Gould-Lardelli, Rongomaiaia Te Whaiti and Reweti Arapere.
funding_verdict: Toi Māori Aotearoa: mainly public: Creative New Zealand, with shop and service income

name: Sarjeant Gallery
overview: Public art gallery, officially Te Whare o Rehua Sarjeant Gallery, at 4 Pukenamu Drive in Pukenamu Queen's Park in the centre of Whanganui.

Founded through the bequest of Henry Sarjeant, who in 1912 left a sum the gallery puts at the equivalent of over $70 million in today's terms. The gallery first opened to the public on 6 September 1919 (the gallery's website).
Holds a collection of more than 8,000 items covering about four centuries of European and New Zealand art.
funding_verdict: Sarjeant Gallery (Whanganui): public and charitable: Whanganui District Council, central government and trusts

name: Centro de Arte Fundación Ortiz-Gurdián
overview: Private non-profit art centre in León, in colonial-era houses opposite the San Francisco church. The foundation also runs a second centre in Managua, in the ground floor of Edificio Málaga, Plaza España.
The Fundación Ortiz-Gurdián was founded in 1996 by the collectors Patricia Gurdián de Ortiz and Ramiro Ortiz Mayorga. The León centre opened in 2000 in the Norberto Ramírez house (DANTEmag, 2015).

The León centre occupies six houses built between the 18th and 19th centuries: Norberto Ramírez, Derbyshire, Martha Juárez, Francisco Juárez, Deshon and Delgadillo (foundation website). DANTEmag dates the Derbyshire house to September 2002 and the restored Delgadillo house to December 2006, and says the Ortiz Gurdián family bought and restored four of the houses from 1999.
funding_verdict: Centro de Arte Fundación Ortiz-Gurdián: private family foundation: founders' money and Banpro sponsorship
wider_context: Nicaraguan police arrested Luis Alberto Rivas Anduray, general manager of Banpro, on the night of Tuesday 15 June 2021 (Infobae, 16 June 2021). The police accused him of inciting foreign interference in internal affairs and calling for military interventions, and cited the law on defending the people's rights to independence, sovereignty and self-determination for peace, approved by the National Assembly in December 2020.

Banpro sponsored the opening of the foundation's Managua centre, and Ramiro Ortiz Mayorga, a co-founder of the foundation, is Banpro's president. The police action was against the sponsor's general manager, not the foundation.

name: Musée National Boubou Hama
overview: Niger's national museum, in a park in central Niamey with a cultural section, a scientific section and a zoo (Wikipedia).

Founded on 18 December 1959 as the Musée National du Niger. Its first conservator, Pablo Toucet, designed it as part of the Culture Valley of Niamey, an idea proposed by Boubou Hama, after whom the museum is named (Wikipedia).
Five traditional houses represent the Fulani, Hausa, Songhai, Tuareg and Zarma peoples, and the museum has a centre for arts and crafts and hosts temporary exhibitions (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Musée National Boubou Hama: state museum of Niger, with international donations planned for a renovation

name: National Museum, Lagos
overview: National museum at Onikan on Lagos Island, administered by the National Commission for Museums and Monuments (Wikipedia).
Founded in 1957 by the English archaeologist Kenneth Murray to preserve Nigeria's historical artefacts (Wikipedia).

Holds an estimated 47,000 objects in wood, ivory, metal and terracotta, among them Nok-culture heads, Benin ivories, Igbo-Ukwu bronzes, Egungun costumes and Akwete cloth. A virtual tour built on an adapted Google Street View was added in 2018 (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: National Museum, Lagos: administered by the National Commission for Museums and Monuments, with IHS Nigeria as 2026 renovation sponsor

name: Yemisi Shyllon Museum of Art
overview: University art museum on the main campus of Pan-Atlantic University in Lekki, Lagos State (Wikipedia).

Founded through an agreement between the university and the collector Prince Yemisi Shyllon, signed in June 2015 after he proposed in September 2014 to house works from his collection there. It opened to the public in October 2019 (Wikipedia). The Art Newspaper reported the opening for 19 October 2019.

Named for Shyllon. The agreement covered his donation of more than 1,000 artworks, taken from the 7,000 works of his Omooba Yemisi Adedoyin Shyllon Art Foundation, created in 2007 (Wikipedia, The Art Newspaper).
funding_verdict: Yemisi Shyllon Museum of Art: privately endowed university museum: the collector Yemisi Shyllon, with 2026 free admission paid by Aisha and Gbenga Oyebode

name: Kunsthall Stavanger
overview: Contemporary art kunsthall at Madlaveien 33 in the Eiganes district of Stavanger, a 10 to 15 minute walk from the city centre and the main bus and train station.

Founded in 1865 as Stavanger kunstforening (Stavanger Art Association) by a group of citizens, with 62 original members and the consul and amateur artist Jens Zetlitz Kielland as first chairman. In 2012 the association's board and general assembly decided to become a kunsthall with an international programme, and it reopened as Kunsthall Stavanger in 2013 with a show by Lina Viste Grønli.

Building: opened by King Haakon VII in 1925 as part of Stavanger's 800th anniversary and the city's first exhibition space for visual art. Designed by the Stavanger architect Erik Erga and built with private funds from individuals and companies.
funding_verdict: Kunsthall Stavanger: public grants and foundation support: Norwegian state, Stavanger municipality and Norwegian foundations

name: Nordnorsk Kunstmuseum
overview: Regional art museum for Northern Norway with three venues: Sjøgata 1 in Tromsø, Storgata 40 in Bodø, and the Nordover Art Center, Road 225-2, Longyearbyen on Svalbard (museum website).

Established as a foundation in 1985 with the Arts Council Norway, the University of Tromsø, the National Gallery and Riksgalleri as initial supporters. Frode Haverkamp was appointed first director in autumn 1986, and the museum opened to the public in February 1988 in rented rooms above the Tromsø Artist's Union at Muségata 2 (museum history page).

Tromsø building: a post and telegraph office designed in 1917 by architect Søren Andreas Wiese Opsahl, used by the Troms police from 1971 to 1996. The museum moved in in December 2001 (museum history page).
funding_verdict: Nordnorsk Kunstmuseum: mainly public: Norwegian state budget, with Nordland county and Bodø municipality for the Bodø venue

name: National Museum of Pakistan
overview: Pakistan's national museum in Burns Garden, on Dr. Ziauddin Ahmed Road, Karachi.
Sources differ on its start: Wikipedia gives 1950 for its establishment and 1951 for the first display in Frere Hall, where it replaced the Victoria Museum; Dawn dates the museum to 1969.
It moved to the present building in 1970.
funding_verdict: National Museum of Pakistan: public: the federal government, in a standing dispute with Sindh province
wider_context: On 24 June 2024 Sindh culture minister Zulfiqar Ali Shah said the museum was "in a dilapidated condition" and that the Centre should hand it to the province for better upkeep (Express Tribune).
Sindh's antiquities department called the earlier federal takeover unconstitutional (The News, 2013).

name: A.M. Qattan Foundation
overview: Cultural and educational development organisation based in Ramallah, West Bank, registered in the UK as a charity (number 1029450) with company number 02171893 (foundation site footer).
Established in London in 1993 by the Palestinian philanthropist Abdel Mohsin Al-Qattan. His son Omar Al-Qattan chairs it (The Art Newspaper, 25 June 2018; Wikipedia).

Building: the Qattan Cultural Centre in Ramallah, designed by the Spanish firm Donaire Arquitectos and due to open to the public on 28 June 2018, with an area of about 7,700 square metres (The Art Newspaper, 25 June 2018). Completion was scheduled for 2016, but security and construction problems delayed it (The Art Newspaper).
funding_verdict: A.M. Qattan Foundation: mainly family-funded, with Swedish funding for a visual arts programme
